name: Windows - Port Forwarding with Netsh
command: netsh.exe interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=<listen_port> listenaddress=<pivot_ip> connectport=<target_port> connectaddress=<target_ip>
description: Uses the built-in netsh portproxy on a Windows pivot to forward a listening port to an internal target - no tools to upload. Connect to the pivot's <listen_port> to reach <target_ip>:<target_port>. Requires an administrator prompt.
source: CPTS Module 12: Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding

examples.label: netsh portproxy
examples.command: netsh.exe interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=8080 listenaddress=10.129.15.150 connectport=3389 connectaddress=172.16.5.25

examples.label: OSCP Ch18 — netsh portproxy for SSH: expose internal SSH on external interface
examples.command: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=2222 listenaddress=<pivot_external_ip> connectport=22 connectaddress=<internal_ip>

examples.label: OSCP Ch18 — open Windows firewall for the portproxy listener port
examples.command: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="port_forward_ssh_2222" protocol=TCP dir=in localip=<pivot_ip> localport=2222 action=allow

examples.label: OSCP Ch18 — verify the portproxy is listening
OSCP Ch18 — cleanup: delete firewall rule and portproxy (always run during cleanup)
examples.command:
netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="port_forward_ssh_2222"
netsh interface portproxy del v4tov4 listenport=2222 listenaddress=<pivot_ip>

notes: `netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4` turns a compromised Windows host into a port forwarder without extra tools (native LOLBIN) - relay an internal service out through the pivot. Remember to open the firewall and delete the rule during cleanup. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 18 (Port Redirection and SSH Tunneling). OSCP Ch18: portproxy alone is not enough — you MUST also open the Windows firewall with netsh advfirewall. Verify the rule with netstat -anp TCP | find "<port>". The portproxy rule persists across reboots (written to registry). Always clean up: delete the firewall rule first, then del the portproxy, and confirm with portproxy show all.

defense.why_it_works: netsh interface portproxy adds a Windows port-forwarding rule (v4tov4) so the pivot relays a local port to an internal host:port - a native, no-tool forwarder.
defense.prerequisites: Admin on a Windows pivot that can reach the internal target.
defense.impact: A native port forward through the Windows pivot to an internal service.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1090.001] A compromised host relaying traffic between segments it shouldn't bridge; an unexpected listening port (SOCKS/forwarder) on the pivot; the pivot initiating connections to hosts/ports it never normally contacts; lateral flows that appear to originate from the pivot (NetFlow/east-west monitoring).
defense.artifacts: A netsh portproxy rule (persisted in registry); the pivot relaying to the internal host.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1090.001 M1030 Network Segmentation] strict east-west firewall rules so one foothold can't reach other segments; egress filtering; IDS/IPS + NetFlow analysis for proxy patterns and long-lived flows; alert on unexpected listeners on servers.
defense.evasion: Uses a built-in Windows feature (no dropped tool); the portproxy rule persists but looks like admin config.
defense.misconfiguration: The network lacks proper segmentation — a compromised DMZ host has direct layer-3 reachability to internal infrastructure (database servers, DCs, internal admin panels). No egress filtering blocks outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to arbitrary hosts, allowing C2 channels and reverse tunnels. Internal firewalls only filter inbound traffic, not east-west or outbound.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Network design: flat Layer-3 network, all VLANs can reach each other
# DMZ web server can ping/connect to: 10.10.10.0/24 (internal LAN), 10.10.20.0/24 (DB subnet)
# No egress proxy — direct outbound HTTP to any IP allowed

# iptables on pivot host (none blocking outbound):
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules

# This allows: chisel client 10.10.10.5:8080 R:socks
# Attacker now has SOCKS5 access to the entire internal network
defense.secure_config:
# Network segmentation with explicit allow rules:
# DMZ -> Internet: only specific egress IPs (patch servers, DNS)
# DMZ -> Internal: ONLY the DB ports this specific app needs
# Internal -> Internal: segment by tier (web tier can't reach DC directly)

# Egress filtering — block all outbound except known-good:
# FortiGate / Palo Alto / iptables:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 8.8.8.8 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT  # DNS to specific server
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_update_servers> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# IDS/IPS signatures for Chisel, ngrok, frp traffic patterns
# DNS monitoring — detect DNS tunneling (dnscat2) via unusual query frequency/length
# HTTP proxy with TLS inspection — detect reverse tunnels in HTTPS streams
